text: Hartung–Knapp adjustment — Adjusts pooled-mean uncertainty using residual scale q and t(k−1); intervals can narrow without a safeguard. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.4.
Restricted maximum likelihood — Estimates heterogeneity accounting for fitted means. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.4.
DerSimonian–Laird estimator — Moment-based estimate of heterogeneity. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.4.
Paule–Mandel estimator — Matches weighted residual variation to degrees of freedom. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.4.

I-squared — Heterogeneity percentage, not magnitude; values depend on estimator. Rough, overlapping bands: 0–40% may be unimportant, 30–60% moderate, 50–90% substantial, 75–100% considerable. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.2.
Between-study variance — Variance of underlying effects on the squared analysis scale. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.3.
Prediction interval — Approximate range for a true effect in a similar setting. The t-based 95% form is μ ± t(k−1)√(SE²+τ²); methods differ. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.3; metafor predict.rma.
Standardised mean difference — Difference between group means divided by a standard deviation; Hedges' g corrects small-sample bias.
Odds ratio — Ratio of the odds of an event in two groups; usually pooled on the log scale and distinct from a risk ratio.
Risk ratio — Risk in one group divided by risk in another; one indicates equal risks.
Hazard ratio — Ratio of instantaneous event rates among those still at risk; interpretation as one constant ratio assumes proportional hazards.
Risk difference — Risk in one group minus risk in another; zero means equal risks.
Network meta-analysis — Combines direct and indirect comparisons of multiple interventions. Cochrane Handbook §11.1.
Surface under the cumulative ranking curve — Summarizes ranking; consider effect sizes and uncertainty too. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.3.3.
Precision of treatment hierarchy — Summarizes dispersion of treatment ranking scores; a flat ranking gives little separation, and the hierarchy should be interpreted with effect uncertainty.
Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation — Framework for rating certainty of evidence.
Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis — GRADE-aligned framework for rating certainty in NMA.
Risk of Bias 2 (Cochrane RCT) — Domain-based tool for assessing risk of bias in randomised trials.
Risk of Bias in Non-randomised Studies of Interventions — Cochrane tool for non-randomised interventional studies.
Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 — Domain-based tool for risk of bias in diagnostic accuracy studies.
A MeaSurement Tool to Assess systematic Reviews 2 — 16-item appraisal tool for systematic reviews.
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses — Reporting checklist + flow diagram for SRs/MAs.
Risk of Bias due to Missing Evidence (Cochrane Ch.13, 2024+) — Per-MA reporting-bias tool; replaces funnel/Egger as the verdict.
INSPECT-SR (Cochrane Oct 2025) — Trustworthiness assessment for primary trials in an SR.
Diagnostic odds ratio — Ratio of the positive to negative likelihood ratio; summarizes discrimination but does not separate sensitivity and specificity.
Summary ROC curve — Summarizes the sensitivity–false-positive-rate relationship across studies under a diagnostic model; not necessarily one achievable operating point.
Hierarchical summary ROC model — Models diagnostic accuracy, threshold and study heterogeneity; parameter definitions depend on the chosen formulation.
Trial sequential analysis — Sequential boundary method for meta-analysis with monitoring boundaries (O'Brien-Fleming).
Minimal important difference — Smallest change perceived as important by patients.
Minimal clinically important difference — Synonymous with MID; emphasises clinical meaningfulness.
Restricted mean survival time — Time-to-event summary up to a fixed horizon τ*; pool differences, not ratios.
Individual patient data — Trial-level participant-level dataset; gold standard for meta-analysis.
Intention-to-treat — Analysis principle: analyse participants as randomised.
Randomised controlled trial — Experimental design with random allocation to interventions.
Credible interval — Interval containing a stated posterior probability for a parameter, conditional on the data, prior and model.
Confidence interval — An interval procedure with a stated long-run coverage rate under its assumptions; it does not assign a probability to the fixed true effect.
Effective sample size — Estimates how much independent-sample information is represented by correlated simulation draws; assess it alongside Monte Carlo error and other diagnostics.
Potential scale reduction (R̂) — Compares within- and between-chain variation to help assess simulation convergence; a value near one alone does not establish reliable posterior inference.
Meta-analytic-predictive prior — Bayesian prior derived from historical trials (Neuenschwander 2010).
PET–PEESE — Conditionally uses PET or PEESE according to a specified test of the PET intercept; a sensitivity analysis, not a guarantee of bias removal.
Graphical display of study heterogeneity — Shows pooled estimates and heterogeneity over subsets; clusters suggest sensitivity patterns, not proof of distinct populations.
Egger's test — Regression test for small-study effects; not proof of publication bias. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.4.
Peters' test — A small-study-effect regression test for binary outcomes. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.4.
Copas selection model — Sensitivity model for selective study availability; conclusions depend on selection assumptions usually not identifiable from the observed studies alone.
Trim-and-fill — Imputes studies to restore funnel symmetry; a sensitivity analysis relying on strong assumptions. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.5.
Bucher indirect comparison — Indirect treatment effect via a common comparator.
Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome — Question framework for systematic reviews.
Evidence-based medicine — Clinical practice informed by best available research evidence.
PROSPERO — International prospective register of systematic reviews.
Cochrane Collaboration — International network producing systematic reviews of healthcare interventions.
Schoenfeld residuals test — Proportional-hazards diagnostic. If rejected, single HR is misleading.
Guyot reconstruction — Algorithm to reconstruct IPD from a Kaplan-Meier curve.
Fragility index — Number of event-status changes required to cross a specified significance threshold under the stated algorithm; depends on the model and permitted changes.
Not positive definite — Covariance-matrix pathology. Fix with nearPD() (Higham), not eigenvalue clamping.
Clopper–Pearson interval — Binomial confidence interval obtained by inverting exact tests; coverage is at least nominal under the binomial model and can be conservative.
Clopper–Pearson interval — Binomial confidence interval obtained by inverting exact tests; coverage is at least nominal under the binomial model and can be conservative.
True positive — Diseased individuals correctly classified as test-positive (cell a of the 2×2 table).
False positive — Non-diseased individuals incorrectly classified as test-positive (cell b).
False negative — Diseased individuals incorrectly classified as test-negative (cell c).
True negative — Non-diseased individuals correctly classified as test-negative (cell d).
Sensitivity — Proportion with the target condition correctly identified as test-positive: TP/(TP+FN).
Specificity — Proportion without the target condition correctly identified as test-negative: TN/(TN+FP).
False-positive rate — Proportion without the target condition who test positive: FP/(FP+TN), equal to 1−specificity.
Receiver operating characteristic — Curve of sensitivity vs 1 − specificity across decision thresholds.
Ordinary least squares — Linear-regression fit minimising squared residuals; used for the Moses-Littenberg SROC line.
Diagnostic test accuracy — Describes how well a test distinguishes those with and without a target condition.
Bayesian inference — Inference framework combining prior beliefs with data via Bayes' theorem.
Frequentist inference — Inference framework based on long-run sampling distributions.
Funnel plot — Plots effects against precision or study size; asymmetry has several possible causes besides missing results. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.2.
Forest plot — Displays study estimates and uncertainty intervals, often alongside a pooled estimate.
Treatment network — Treatments linked by available direct comparisons. Cochrane Handbook §11.1.
Indirect evidence — Comparison through other network interventions. Cochrane Handbook §11.1.
Multi-arm study — A study comparing more than two interventions; estimates sharing a comparator are dependent.
Subgroup analysis — Compares effects across study groups. Cochrane Handbook §10.11.2.
Sensitivity analysis — Repeats an analysis using alternative assumptions or choices to assess how much the conclusions depend on them.
Cumulative meta-analysis — Updates a pooled estimate as studies enter in a specified order; repeated looks need care when interpreting significance.
Influence analysis — Examines how fitted results change when a study is removed or perturbed.
Heterogeneity — Variation in underlying effects across studies, which may reflect differences in populations, methods or interventions.
Bias — Systematic deviation from the truth. Distinguish from random error.
Statistical power — Probability of detecting an effect when one exists.
Type I error — False positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis.
Type II error — False negative: failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
Effect size — A numerical measure of a difference or association, such as a risk ratio or mean difference.
Pooled estimate — A model-based combination of study estimates; its interpretation depends on the effect scale and pooling assumptions.
Meta-regression — Relates study effects to study characteristics; associations need not be causal. Cochrane Handbook §10.11.4.
Mixed-effects meta-regression — Random-effects MA + covariates; default in metafor.
Confounder adjustment — Statistical control for confounding variables.
Calibration (prediction model) — Agreement between predicted and observed risks.
Discrimination (prediction model) — Ability to rank cases above non-cases (AUC).
Net benefit (decision curve) — Decision-analytic summary of clinical utility across thresholds.
Quality-adjusted life year — Health-economic outcome combining length + quality of life.
Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio — Cost per QALY gained between interventions.
Cochran's Q — Tests variation against sampling error; low power with few studies. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.2.
Fixed-effect model — Assumes one underlying effect. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.1.
Random-effects model — Models a distribution of underlying effects. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.4.1.
Standard error — Estimated sampling variability of an estimate; a smaller SE means greater precision under the model.
Standard deviation — Describes how much individual values vary around their mean; distinct from the standard error of that mean.
P-value — Probability, assuming the null model, of a result at least as extreme as observed; not the probability that the null is true.
Degrees of freedom — Amount of independent information used to estimate a variance or determine a reference distribution.
Normal z statistic — An estimate minus its null value divided by its standard error, compared with a standard normal distribution.
Student's t statistic — A standardized estimate compared with a t distribution using stated degrees of freedom, which affect tail probabilities.
Chi-squared statistic — A nonnegative statistic compared with a chi-squared distribution with stated degrees of freedom for tests such as heterogeneity or association.
Number of studies — Number of studies contributing to an analysis; with dependent effects, the number of independent study clusters matters.
Sample size — Number of participants or observations; for incidence-rate data the denominator may instead be person-time.
Study weight — A study's contribution to a pooled estimate, usually determined by precision and the chosen model.
Inverse-variance weighting — Combines estimates using weights inversely related to their variance, adding heterogeneity variance in a random-effects model.
Harbord's test — A score-based regression test for small-study effects with binary outcomes. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.4.
Begg's rank correlation test — Checks association between effects and their variances using ranks; a nonsignificant result does not exclude small-study effects.
Small-study effects — Differences between smaller and larger studies, potentially caused by bias, heterogeneity or chance. Cochrane Handbook §13.3.4.
Publication bias — Selective publication related to findings can distort the available evidence. Cochrane Handbook §13.1.
Precision-effect test — Regresses effects on standard errors using inverse-variance weights; the intercept extrapolates to zero sampling error and may be unstable.
Precision-effect estimate with standard error — Regresses effects on sampling variances; the intercept extrapolates to zero sampling variance and depends on model assumptions.
Limit meta-analysis — Extrapolates a model relating effect and precision to zero sampling error; the limit estimate depends on model assumptions and available study sizes.
Selection model — Models how availability of study results depends on findings; adjusted estimates depend on unverifiable selection assumptions.
Log risk ratio — Natural logarithm of a risk ratio; zero means equal risks and exponentiating returns the risk ratio.
Log odds ratio — Natural logarithm of an odds ratio; zero means equal odds and exponentiating returns the odds ratio.
Incidence rate ratio — Ratio of event rates per person-time; distinct from a ratio of cumulative risks.
Mean difference — Difference between group means on the same outcome scale.
Proportion — Number with an event divided by the total observed, between zero and one; here p denotes a proportion, not a test p-value.
Logit transformation — Logarithm of p/(1−p), mapping a probability between zero and one to the real line; undefined at exactly zero or one.
Freeman–Tukey transformation — Double-arcsine transformation for pooling proportions; back-transformed estimates depend on the sample-size convention and can be hard to interpret.
Untransformed proportion — Pools proportions on their original scale; normal approximations may perform poorly near zero or one.
Generalized linear mixed model — Uses a link function and random effects; a binomial-normal model directly models event counts with normally distributed random effects.
Continuity correction — Adds a small count when zero cells prevent a calculation; the choice can affect estimates for sparse data.
Wilson interval — A confidence interval for a binomial proportion obtained by inverting a score test, often better behaved than a simple normal interval.
Maximum likelihood — Estimates parameters by maximizing the likelihood of the observed data under the model.
Method of moments — Estimates parameters by matching observed summary quantities to their expected values.
Variance components — Separate sources of variance in a model; in a method menu this names a moment-based estimator of those components.
Empirical Bayes estimator — Estimates a distribution's parameters from the studies themselves; the heterogeneity estimator here is equivalent to Paule–Mandel.
Sidik–Jonkman estimator — A two-step estimator of between-study variance using standardized study effects; results can differ from other heterogeneity estimators.
Hedges estimator — A moment-based estimator of between-study variance using unweighted variability of study estimates.
Hunter–Schmidt estimator — A moment-based estimator of between-study variance using precision-weighted variation of study estimates.
Between-study standard deviation — Square root of τ², on the same analysis scale as the underlying effects.
H-squared — Conventionally Q/(k−1), matching the DL definition when Q exceeds its degrees of freedom; REML-based H² instead uses estimated heterogeneity and typical sampling variance.
Q-profile interval — Interval for heterogeneity variance obtained by inverting a generalized Q statistic under the model.
Baujat plot — Plots a measure of heterogeneity contribution against influence on the pooled result to highlight studies for investigation.
Leave-one-out analysis — Repeats the analysis with each study omitted to show sensitivity to individual studies; does not justify automatic exclusion.
Residual — Difference between an observed study estimate and the value predicted by the model.
Standardized residual — Residual scaled by an estimated standard deviation to identify observations poorly predicted by the model.
Leverage (hat value) — Measures how much an observation can influence its fitted value, based on its weight and position in the model.
Cook's distance — Summarizes the change in fitted coefficients when a study is omitted; large values suggest influence, not necessarily error.
DFFITS — Standardized change in a study's fitted value when that study is omitted.
DFBETAS — Standardized changes in model coefficients when a study is omitted.
Covariance ratio — Ratio of coefficient covariance determinants with and without a study, indicating its effect on precision.
Median — Middle of an ordered distribution, with half the observations on either side.
Between-subgroup Q — Tests whether subgroup pooled effects differ beyond estimated sampling uncertainty; does not establish a causal subgroup effect.
Heterogeneity explained (R-squared) — Estimated proportional reduction in residual between-study variance after including moderators; can be unstable with few studies.
Residual heterogeneity Q — Tests unexplained variation after accounting for moderators against expected sampling variation.
Residual sum of squares — Sum of squared residuals, with weights where specified; used to estimate dispersion or assess fit.
Moderator or covariate — A study characteristic included to explain effect differences; study-level associations may differ from individual-level associations.
Regression intercept — Predicted effect when all predictors equal zero or their chosen centered reference values.
Regression slope — Change in the predicted effect per unit increase in a predictor, holding other predictors constant.
Regression coefficient — Estimated change associated with a model term on the analysis scale; interpretation depends on coding and other terms.
Interaction — Allows the effect of one predictor or component to depend on another; meaning depends on the analysis scale.
Permutation test — Compares the observed statistic with rearranged data under an exchangeability assumption; simulated permutations add Monte Carlo error.
Location-scale model — Models both the mean effect and residual heterogeneity as functions of covariates.
Multilevel meta-analysis — Models effects nested within studies, allowing variation between studies and between effects within a study.
Within-study effect variance — Variation in underlying effects within a study in a multilevel model, distinct from sampling error and between-study variance.
Between-study variance component — Variation between study-level underlying effects in a multilevel model.
Robust variance estimation — Allows dependent effect estimates within independent study clusters; reliable inference still needs adequate independent clusters and model assumptions.

Bias-reduced cluster-robust variance — A small-sample adjustment to cluster-robust standard errors, used with suitable degrees of freedom; it cannot guarantee reliable inference with very few clusters.
Satterthwaite degrees of freedom — Approximates a t reference distribution for an estimated variance; degrees of freedom can differ by coefficient and be much smaller than the number of studies.
Correlation — Describes the strength and direction of a linear association, from −1 to 1; does not establish causation.
Working correlation — Assumed correlation among effect estimates within a study used to form weights; sensitivity checks assess dependence on this choice.
Condition number — Measures sensitivity of a matrix calculation to small changes; large values indicate potential numerical instability.
Centering predictors — Subtracts a reference value, often the mean, from each predictor to change the intercept's interpretation.
Fisher z transformation — Transforms a correlation r using atanh(r); approximate sampling variance is 1/(n−3) under the usual correlation model.
Pearson correlation — Measures linear association between two variables from −1 to 1; pooling often uses Fisher z before back-transformation.
Covariance — Measures how two quantities vary together; covariance matrices include variances on the diagonal and covariances off the diagonal.
Within-study covariance — Sampling dependence between estimates from one study, used to avoid treating correlated estimates as independent.
Between-study covariance — How the underlying effects for different outcomes vary together across studies.
Multivariate meta-analysis — Jointly pools correlated outcomes using their covariance structure; results depend on within- and between-study covariance assumptions.
Univariate meta-analysis — Pools one outcome at a time without modelling dependence with other outcomes.
Direct evidence — Studies comparing the interventions head to head. Cochrane Handbook §11.1.
Network inconsistency — Disagreement between evidence sources; nonsignificance does not prove agreement. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.4.
Node-splitting — Compares direct and indirect evidence for the same contrast. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.4.2.
Design-by-treatment test — Global assessment of disagreement across network designs. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.4.3.
Transitivity — Comparability of effect modifiers across network comparisons. Cochrane Handbook §11.2.3.1.
P-score — Frequentist ranking summary; not a probability of being best. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.3.3.
Probability of being best — Model-based probability of first rank. Cochrane Handbook §11.4.3.3.
League table — Matrix of pairwise intervention estimates. Cochrane Handbook §11.6.
Treatment contrast — Estimated difference or relative effect comparing two interventions on the analysis scale.
Component network meta-analysis — Models interventions through their components; an additive model assumes component effects add on the chosen outcome scale.
Additive component model — Assumes an intervention's effect equals the sum of its component effects on the specified scale.
Mantel–Haenszel method — Combines binary-outcome tables across studies using stratified weights; the formula depends on the effect measure.
Peto odds ratio — Approximate odds-ratio method using observed minus expected events; performance can be poor with large effects or unequal group sizes.
Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test — Tests association in stratified binary tables; distinct from testing heterogeneity of study effects.
Breslow–Day test — Tests whether odds ratios vary across strata beyond sampling variation, conditional on a common-odds-ratio model.
Tarone-adjusted test — Adjustment to the Breslow–Day test of homogeneity of odds ratios.
L'Abbé plot — Plots event risks in the two groups against one another to inspect differences among studies.
Fragility quotient — Fragility index divided by the sample-size denominator specified by the analysis.
Bivariate diagnostic model — Jointly models transformed sensitivity and specificity or false-positive rate, allowing correlated heterogeneity between studies.
Positive likelihood ratio — Sensitivity divided by 1−specificity; multiplying pre-test odds by LR+ gives post-test odds after a positive result.
Negative likelihood ratio — (1−sensitivity) divided by specificity; multiplying pre-test odds by LR− gives post-test odds after a negative result.
Diagnostic likelihood ratio — Ratio relating test results in people with and without the condition, used to update pre-test odds.
Area under the ROC curve — Summarizes discrimination across thresholds; partial AUC restricts the false-positive-rate range and requires that range to be specified.
Fagan nomogram — Converts pre-test probability to post-test probability using a diagnostic likelihood ratio.
Deeks' test — Regression test for small-study effects in diagnostic meta-analysis; asymmetry is not proof of publication bias.
Moses–Littenberg SROC — Regression summary of diagnostic accuracy that does not fully model binomial sampling error and between-study variation.
Spearman rank correlation — Measures monotonic association using ranks; a diagnostic threshold association need not establish its cause.
HSROC accuracy parameter — Describes diagnostic discrimination; not the proportion of all tests correctly classified.
Diagnostic threshold — Decision boundary for a positive test, or its model parameter; changing it can trade sensitivity against specificity.
HSROC shape parameter — Controls asymmetry of the modeled summary ROC curve; interpretation depends on the HSROC parameterisation.
HSROC variance components — Between-study variances in the model's threshold and accuracy parameters, distinct from sampling variance.
Log-likelihood — Logarithm of the likelihood under a fitted model; comparisons require compatible data and likelihood conventions.
Akaike information criterion — Balances likelihood fit against parameter count; smaller values favor a model among comparable fits, not proof of correctness.
Small-sample corrected AIC — Adds a finite-sample penalty to AIC; valid comparisons require compatible likelihoods and data.
Bayesian information criterion — Model comparison criterion with a sample-size-dependent complexity penalty; lower values favor a model among compatible fits.
Likelihood-ratio test — Compares nested models through their likelihoods; the reference distribution needs care for variance parameters on a boundary.
Wald test — Compares estimated coefficients with null values using their estimated covariance; relies on the reference approximation.
Dose-response meta-analysis — Pools the exposure dose–outcome relationship, allowing dependence among estimates from one study.
Linear trend — Assumes constant change on the analysis scale per unit increase in dose or a predictor.
Quadratic curve — Includes dose and squared dose terms, allowing curvature determined by their coefficients.
Restricted cubic spline — Smooth piecewise cubic curve joined at knots and constrained to be linear in the tails.
Spline knots — Dose values where spline pieces join; their number and locations affect flexibility.
Greenland–Longnecker method — Reconstructs within-study covariance between dose-category log relative risks sharing a reference group, using counts and reported estimates.
Hamling method — Reconstructs effective counts to approximate covariance of adjusted relative-risk estimates sharing a reference category.
Two-stage estimation — Fits a dose-response model within each study, then pools the coefficients with their covariance matrices.
One-stage estimation — Fits the dose-response relationship across studies in one combined model.
Reference dose — Dose against which relative risks are calculated; changing it changes the comparison, not the fitted curve.
Deviance — Likelihood-based measure of lack of fit relative to a reference model; its meaning and reference distribution depend on the model.
Coefficient of determination — Fraction of observed variability explained by regression; adjusted R² accounts for model size and differs from heterogeneity-explained R².

text: Variance ratio — Ratio of estimated variances, here comparing precision between univariate and multivariate fits.
Case-control study — Samples people according to outcome status and compares prior exposure; odds ratios need appropriate interpretation.
Person-time — Total time participants contribute while at risk, used as the denominator for incidence rates.
Cumulative incidence — Proportion experiencing an event over a specified follow-up period.
Non-linearity test — Tests whether additional curve terms improve on a linear dose relationship under the chosen model.

I-squared — Heterogeneity percentage, not magnitude; values depend on estimator. Rough, overlapping bands: 0–40% may be unimportant, 30–60% moderate, 50–90% substantial, 75–100% considerable. Cochrane Handbook §10.10.2.
Mantel–Haenszel method — Combines binary-outcome tables across studies using stratified weights; the formula depends on the effect measure.
Peto odds ratio — Approximate odds-ratio method using observed minus expected events; performance can be poor with large effects or unequal group sizes.
Network consistency — Agreement between direct and indirect evidence. Cochrane Handbook §11.2.3.2.
Mean effect — Average underlying effect on the analysis scale, estimated by the fitted model.
Sampling variance — Expected squared sampling deviation of an estimate; equals its standard error squared.
Number of effect estimates — Count of effect estimates, which can exceed the number of independent studies when several effects come from each study.
Number of study clusters — Count of independent study groups; effects within a group may be dependent.
Number of coefficients — Count of estimated regression coefficients, including the intercept when present; distinct from a test p-value.
Hartung–Knapp scale factor — Residual-based factor used to adjust coefficient variance; a modified procedure may floor it at one to prevent a smaller standard error.
Log-variance intercept — Predicted log residual heterogeneity variance when the scale-model covariates are zero.
Log-variance slope — Change in log residual heterogeneity variance per unit increase in a scale-model covariate.
Within-study correlation — Dependence between the sampling errors of estimates from the same study; an assumed value should be checked in sensitivity analyses.
Moderator test — Tests whether specified moderator coefficients jointly equal zero under the fitted model.
F statistic — A test statistic compared with an F distribution with numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, often for multiple regression coefficients.
Bootstrap — Repeatedly resamples data to estimate uncertainty; results depend on the resampling unit and assumptions.
Monte Carlo sampling — Uses random draws to approximate an otherwise costly calculation; results have simulation error.
